items.title: Modern Judaism has Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and Reconstructionist branches
items.claim: What distinguishes the main Jewish denominations?

options.text: There are no real denominational differences

Orthodox (Modern Orthodox, Haredi), Conservative (Masorti in UK), Reform, and Reconstructionist — distinguished mainly by their stance on the binding nature of Halakhah (Jewish law) and engagement with modernity

items.reveal:
Reform Judaism emerged in early 19th-century Germany (Israel Jacobson, Abraham Geiger), arguing for adapting tradition to modern reason. Modern Orthodox (Samson Raphael Hirsch) defended strict observance of Halakhah while engaging modern life. Haredi (often called 'ultra-Orthodox') resists much of modernity.

Conservative/Masorti Judaism (Zacharias Frankel, Solomon Schechter at JTS New York from 1902) is a middle path — Halakhah binding but historically developing. Reconstructionist Judaism (Mordecai Kaplan, 1922) sees Judaism as an evolving religious civilisation.

In Israel the Chief Rabbinate is Orthodox and controls marriage and conversion law; in the US, Reform is the largest denomination by membership.
items.why: Religions are internally diverse. Judaism's denominational landscape sets up the central modern question — how do tradition and modernity relate? — in structurally different ways.

items.title: The Torah is the first five books of the Hebrew Bible

options.text: The first five books — Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy — traditionally attributed to Moses; also called the Pentateuch or Chumash

items.reveal:
The Hebrew Bible (Tanakh) has three sections: Torah (Teaching, 5 books), Nevi'im (Prophets, 8 books), Ketuvim (Writings, 11 books). Tanakh is an acronym of those three.

The Torah is read in synagogue in a one-year cycle (annual cycle) or three-year cycle (some Reform congregations). The annual cycle ends and restarts on Simchat Torah.

The written Torah is complemented by the Oral Torah — the rabbinic tradition codified in the Mishnah (around 200 CE) and Talmud (around 500 CE). For Orthodox Judaism, both were revealed at Sinai.
items.why: 'The Torah' as a generic term for Jewish scripture obscures structure. Students need to distinguish Torah, Tanakh and Talmud — and notice that Christian 'Old Testament' is the same content as Tanakh but in different order.

items.title: Diwali has multiple regional meanings

options.text: A single event — Rama's return to Ayodhya

Multiple events depending on region: Rama's return to Ayodhya (north India), Krishna's defeat of Narakasura (south India), Lakshmi's emergence (west India); also marks new year for some Hindu, Jain and Sikh communities

items.reveal:
Diwali (Sanskrit dipavali, 'row of lamps') falls in October-November on the new moon of Kartika. The five-day festival includes Dhanteras (wealth), Naraka Chaturdashi (Krishna's victory), Diwali itself (Lakshmi puja, Rama's return), Govardhan Puja, and Bhai Dooj (siblings).

For Jains, it marks Mahavira's attainment of moksha. For Sikhs, it commemorates Guru Hargobind's release from imprisonment in 1619 (Bandi Chhor Divas).

The festival has become a major UK public event — Leicester's Diwali celebrations are the largest outside India.
items.why: Pan-Hindu festivals can have different narratives in different regions. Treating Diwali as a single myth misses how diverse Hindu practice is and how it links to neighbouring traditions (Jain, Sikh) at the same calendrical moment.
